Interface RouteSpec<S extends RouteSpec<S>>

Type Parameters:
S - The type of the route or the group
All Superinterfaces:
ExecutionSpec<S>, RouteFilterSpec<S>
All Known Subinterfaces:
HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>, HttpRouteGroup, HttpRouteSpec
public sealed interface RouteSpec<S extends RouteSpec<S>> extends RouteFilterSpec<S>, ExecutionSpec<S> permits HttpRouteSpec, HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>, HttpRouteGroup
The settings a handler route, see HttpRouteSpec, and a group of routes, see HttpRouteGroup, share: the media types, the annotations, the attributes, the conditions, the order and the port, besides the filters of RouteFilterSpec and the executor of ExecutionSpec.

On a route, a setting is the value of the route. On a group, it is the default of the routes declared in the lambda of the group, and of its nested groups, wherever it is declared in the lambda, before the routes, after them or in between: a route, or a nested group, with its own value overrides the one of the group, so the innermost value wins. The conditions, the attributes and the annotations of the groups and of the route are combined, see each method.

routes.path("/admin", admin -> admin
    .executeOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING)
    .annotate(Audited.class)
    .GET("/users", (request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(users.findAll())));
Since:
5.3.0
Author:
Denis Stepanov

  • Method Details

    • consumes

      S consumes(MediaType... mediaTypes)
      Accept requests with these media types only, like @Consumes on a controller method, or on a controller for a group.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, consume them instead of application/json. A route that declares what it consumes, with this method or consumesAll(), and a nested group that does, replace them, like a method-level @Consumes replaces the one of its controller. So does a form route, e.g. HttpRouteSpec.form(), which consumes the form media types: a form handler reads a form.

      routes.path("/notes", notes -> {
    notes.consumes(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE).produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE);
    notes.POST("/").body(String.class).handle((request, pathVariables, text) -> HttpResponse.ok(notes.save(text)));
    notes.POST("/json")
        .consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_TYPE)
        .body(Note.class).handle((request, pathVariables, note) -> HttpResponse.ok(notes.save(note)));
});

      The media types, and the executor, see ExecutionSpec.executeOn(String), of a group apply to its routes to handlers, including the implicit HEAD routes, the routes declared for several methods and the declared routes, not to its error and status routes.

      Parameters:
      mediaTypes - The media types
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • annotationMetadata

      S annotationMetadata(AnnotationMetadataProvider annotationMetadata)
      Give the route the annotations of an annotated element: the features that read the annotations of the matched route, such as security rules, versioning, filter binding, route conditions and the message body writers, see them as if they were on a controller method, and so does the return type of the route.

      When the element is an ExecutableMethod, e.g. a method of a resource that a framework integration routes with handler functions, the route implements that bean method: besides its annotations, the target method, declaring type and method name of the route are the ones of the bean method, so the local @Error methods of the bean class apply to the route, and the route is described as the bean method. The arguments of the route stay those of the handler. Any other element, e.g. a BeanDefinition, gives the route its annotations only.

      ExecutableMethod<Payments, String> pay = beanContext.getBeanDefinition(Payments.class).getRequiredMethod("pay", long.class);
routes.POST("/payments/{amount}")
    .annotationMetadata(pay)
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(payments.pay(pathVariables.getLong("amount"))));

      The route keeps the element: an integration finds it back on the matched route with MethodBasedRouteInfo.getAnnotationMetadataProvider(), and the bean method of the route with instanceof ExecutableMethod. The last element given to the route wins.

      On a group, the element is the default element of the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, to handlers: a route without its own element has the one of its innermost group that has one, as if it were given to the route, e.g. the BeanDefinition of a resource for every route of the resource. The element of a route, or of a nested group, replaces it. The annotations given with annotate(AnnotationValue) to the groups and to the route override the ones of the element.

      Parameters:
      annotationMetadata - The annotated element whose annotations the route has, an ExecutableMethod for a route that implements a bean method
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • annotate

      <T extends Annotation> S annotate(AnnotationValue<T> annotationValue)
      Annotate the route with an annotation, like an annotation on a controller method, with the annotate methods of the compile-time elements, e.g. io.micronaut.inject.ast.Element#annotate: the features that read the annotations of the matched route see it, e.g. a @FilterMatcher annotation binds its filters to the route, and @Version selects the route by the version of the request. Several annotations are chained calls. 
      routes.POST("/payments/{amount}")
    .annotate(Audited.class)
    .annotate(Version.class, version -> version.value("2"))
    .handle(payHandler);

      If the route already has the annotation, the members of the given one are merged with, and override, the existing ones; a repeatable annotation is added to the existing ones. The annotations of the route are layered like the annotations of a controller method over the ones of its class: the annotations of the element given with annotationMetadata(AnnotationMetadataProvider), then of the groups of the route, outer group first, then of the route, each overriding the members of the same annotation before it.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, have the annotation; the annotation of a nested group or of a route overrides the members it sets.

      The meta-annotations of an annotation type are not known at runtime: a feature that looks up an annotation by its own type sees it, like the ones above, @CrossOrigin, @ExecuteOn or a security annotation, but a feature that looks up a stereotype of the annotation needs the stereotype in the annotation value, see AnnotationValueBuilder.stereotype(AnnotationValue). The expressions of an annotation, e.g. of @RouteCondition, are compiled with the annotated code: a route condition is declared with where(RouteCondition).

      Type Parameters:
      T - The annotation type
      Parameters:
      annotationValue - The annotation
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • attribute

      S attribute(String name, Object value)
      Give the route an attribute: metadata of the route for the code that handles its requests, which reads it from the matched route with RouteInfo.getAttribute(String), e.g. a route filter, a server filter or the handler. They are the attributes of the route, not of the request, see RouteAttributes for the route of a request.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, have the attribute; the attribute of a nested group or of a route with the same name overrides it.

      routes.path("/admin", admin -> {
    admin.attribute("role", "admin");
    admin.GET("/users", usersHandler);
    admin.GET("/audit").attribute("role", "auditor").handle(auditHandler);
});
routes.serverFilter("/admin/**").beforeReplacing(request -> {
    String role = RouteAttributes.getRouteInfo(request)
        .flatMap(route -> route.getAttribute("role", String.class))
        .orElseThrow();
    return hasRole(request, role) ? null : HttpResponse.status(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
});
      Parameters:
      name - The name of the attribute
      value - The value of the attribute
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • where

      S where(RouteCondition condition)
      Match the requests that meet a condition only, like @RouteCondition on a controller method: a request the condition rejects is answered as if the route did not exist, by another route of the same URI and method, e.g. one with another condition, or by 404, never by a 405, 415 or 406 of this route. The conditions are evaluated while the request is matched, for every request whose path the route matches: they must be fast and must not block, nor read the body. 
      routes.GET("/reports/{id}")
    .where(RouteCondition.header("X-Export", "csv"))
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(reports.csv(pathVariables.getLong("id"))));
routes.GET("/reports/{id}", (request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(reports.find(pathVariables.getLong("id"))));

      A request both routes of the example match, with the header, is ambiguous: the most specific route answers it, and the two routes are equally specific, so it is answered with 400. RouteCondition builds conditions on the headers, query parameters, cookies, method, host, client address and time of the request, and RequestPredicates on its media types too.

      On a group, the condition applies to the routes of the group, including the routes of its nested groups: a route matches a request that meets the conditions of its groups and its own, which must all be met, as one all condition. Several conditions of a route or a group must all be met too. The router evaluates them cheapest first, the custom conditions last, in the order they were declared, outer group first.

      Parameters:
      condition - The condition
      Returns:
      The route or the group
      Since:
      5.3.0

    • where

      default S where(Predicate<HttpRequest<?>> condition)
      Match the requests that meet a condition of a lambda only, see where(RouteCondition): a custom condition, which the router cannot read and evaluates after the others. The lambda is given the request as it is: it reads the Host header and the peer of the connection, not the host and the client address the server resolves, which only the conditions of RouteCondition read.
      Parameters:

      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • constrain

      S constrain(Predicate<? super PathVariables> accepted)
      Constrain the path variables of the route: the route matches a request only when the constraint accepts the path variables its URI template bound. Otherwise the route is not a match, as if its URI template did not match: the request goes on to the other routes, e.g. a route with the same URI template, or is answered with 404 when none matches. 
      routes.path("/shops/{shop}", shop -> shop
    .constrain("shop", SHOPS)
    .GET("/stock", stockHandler));
routes.GET("/orders/{id}")
    .constrain("id", Long.class, id -> id > 0)
    .handle(ordersHandler);

      A constraint runs while the request is matched, after the URI template of the route matched and bound the variables, before the media types, the conditions, see where(RouteCondition), and the ambiguity between the routes are considered. It is given the same PathVariables the handler is given. Since a rejected route is not a match, the methods allowed on a path for a 405, the media types for a 415 or 406, a CORS preflight request and the implicit HEAD route consider only the routes whose constraints pass: a rejected value never produces a 405. A constraint that throws an exception, e.g. a variable that does not convert, rejects the variables; the exception is logged at debug level.

      A constraint should be cheap, and must not have side effects: it runs for every request the URI template of the route matches, including the requests another route answers. A route without constraints costs nothing more to match.

      On a group, the constraint applies to the routes of the group, including the routes of its nested groups: the constraints of the groups, outer group first, and of the route must all pass.

      Parameters:
      accepted - Whether the path variables are accepted
      Returns:
      The route or the group
      Since:
      5.3.0

    • order

      S order(int order)
      Break a tie with other routes that are equally good for a request: the route with the lowest order answers it. The router keeps the routes that explicitly produce the media type the request accepts first, then, for a request with a body, the routes that explicitly consume its content type, then the routes with the most specific URI template; it then prefers a route of the request's method over a route of any method, and an explicit HEAD route over an implicit one; only the routes still left after that are compared by their order. So the order never makes a less specific route, or a route of any method over a route of the request's method, win: it chooses among routes of the same URI template whose conditions a request both meets, e.g. a specialized route and a fallback. Two routes left with the same order still make the request ambiguous, answered with 400. 
      routes.GET("/reports/{id}")
    .where(RequestPredicates.queryParam("format", "csv"))
    .order(-1)
    .handle(csvHandler);
routes.GET("/reports/{id}", reportHandler); // the order 0: answers the other requests

      The order is global: it is compared between any routes left for a request, controller routes and the routes of every HttpRoutes bean and group alike, and the lower order wins. The default order is 0, the order of a controller route, so a route with a negative order wins a tie with a controller route and one with a positive order loses it. On a group, the order is the default of the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, unless they or a nested group have their own. The order of an HttpRoutes bean orders the beans, not their routes.

      Parameters:
      order - The order, lower wins
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • port

      S port(int port)
      Route the requests on this port only, like @Controller(port = ...): the server opens the port when it starts, and the route does not match a request on another port, which is answered as if the route did not exist. A route without a port matches the requests on the default ports of the server only, once a route of the application has a port. 
      routes.GET("/metrics")
    .port(9090)
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(metrics.scrape()));

      On a group, the routes of the group, including the routes of its nested groups, inherit the port; a nested group or a route with its own port overrides it.

      Parameters:
      port - The port, between 1 and 65535: unlike @Controller(port = ...), a negative port or 0, a random port the route could not match, is rejected
      Returns:
      The route or the group
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if the port is not between 1 and 65535

    • port

      S port(String port)
      Route the requests on the port of a property, like @Controller(port = "${my.admin.port}"), whose port member is a string: a number, or an expression with property placeholders, with defaults, e.g. ${my.admin.port:8081}, resolved with the environment of the application like the port of a controller, when the routes are declared. Otherwise the same as port(int), on a route and on a group. 
      routes.GET("/metrics").port("${management.port:9090}").handle(metricsHandler);
      Parameters:
      port - The port, or an expression that resolves to it
      Returns:
      The route or the group
      Throws:
      ConfigurationException - if a placeholder cannot be resolved
      IllegalArgumentException - if the port is not a number between 1 and 65535
